The Stigma of Sadness: Depression and Public Life
As Abraham Lincoln’s public life took off, so did the attention on his emotional world.
Imagine living in a time when society prized stoicism—where showing emotion meant risking your reputation. Lincoln’s bouts of melancholy weren’t just whispered about; they became a public talking point. Some folks wondered out loud if he was fit to lead. Others quietly questioned his stability.
The truth is, back then, depression carried a heavy stigma. Lincoln could feel the weight of it.
In politics, his rivals didn’t hesitate to use it against him. They’d call him unstable, not tough enough for the harsh world of politics. Meanwhile, supporters tried to spin his sadness, saying he was simply “thoughtful” or “serious-minded.” But let’s be honest—the reality was far more complex. Lincoln’s sadness wasn’t a weakness; it was a sign of just how deeply he cared about the world’s pain.
Most people, when faced with this kind of scrutiny, would probably try to hide their struggles. Lincoln, though, didn’t play that game. He didn’t pretend to be cheerful if he wasn’t. He’d talk openly about his pain—sometimes using humor to ease the tension, but never denying what he felt.
In a world where emotional pain was swept under the rug, that kind of honesty was rare—and honestly, a little refreshing.
Still, Lincoln was smart about it. He knew he couldn’t share everything. In a culture that saw emotional steadiness as strength, he had to strike a delicate balance. He shared enough to be genuine, but not so much that he’d undermine his authority. That takes courage, doesn’t it? To be vulnerable, but not exposed.
The stigma around depression didn’t just affect Lincoln, though—it shaped how everyone saw mental health. Back then, there was little understanding of what it meant to struggle inside. If you felt sad or anxious, people often thought there was something wrong with you. There weren’t many resources, and even fewer role models to show that you could still live—and lead—while carrying that burden.
Lincoln changed that narrative, simply by being himself. He showed us you can be both vulnerable and strong—wounded, but wise. He never let his pain define him, but he didn’t hide it either. Instead, he turned his suffering into a source of empathy and insight, using it to connect with others on a deeper level.
Looking back, it’s clear: Lincoln’s willingness to face the stigma of sadness was one of his bravest acts. He didn’t just bear his own pain—he changed the way people thought about suffering. For him, depression wasn’t a secret shame. It was a reality he met with honesty and compassion, challenging us all to rethink what it means to be strong.
